en: The Chapter on Falsity (Vaitathya-prakaraṇa).
It has been stated that when [reality] is known, duality does not exist.
“[Brahman is] one only, without a second” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and so forth— from such scriptural passages [this follows]; that is merely based on tradition (āgama).
In this regard, since the unreality of duality can also be ascertained through the mode of birth, the second chapter begins:
"The wise declare that all things are unreal in a dream, because objects exist within [the self] and because they are enclosed. (MandU 2.1)
*Vaitathya* is the state of being false; that is to say, unreality.
Of what? Of all external and internal entities, of all things perceived in a dream.
The wise, who are skilled in the means of valid cognition, say— that is, they declare—
the reason for its unreality to be its abiding within [the internal].
Those whose location is within the interior of the body—
for it is there that entities such as mountains and elephants are perceived, and not outside the body—
therefore they ought to be unreal.
Anticipating the objection that the reason is inconclusive because of jars and other objects perceived inside enclosed spaces such as rooms, he says, "by the reason of being enclosed.
This means "because of being in an internally enclosed place.
For it is not possible for mountains, elephants, and so forth to exist within the channels inside the body, which is itself enclosed.
For there is no mountain in the body. //1//

Regarding the claim that the objects seen in dreams have their locus concealed within, this is unproven; for, having raised the objection that one who has fallen asleep appears as if seeing dreams with his eyes wide open, [the author] says: START MandUpK 2.2: "The claim that the objects seen in dreams have their locus concealed within is unproven, because one who has previously fallen asleep is seen as if seeing dreams with his eyes wide open. Thus he speaks, having raised this doubt.
And because the duration of time is not long, having gone to those places, he does not see them;
and indeed, upon awakening, that entire place is no longer found.
One does not go to another place outside the body to see dreams;
for, as soon as one has fallen asleep, one appears as if seeing dreams in a location hundreds of *yojanas* away from the site of the body— a place that would take a full month to reach—
and there is no long duration of time for the journey to and from that place.
Therefore, because of the great length of time, the dreamer does not travel to another place.
Furthermore, every dreamer upon waking is not found in the location where the dream was seen.
Moreover, if one were to travel to another place during a dream, one would awaken in that very place where one had been seeing the dreams.
And this is not the case:
one who is asleep at night sees entities as if during the day,
and becomes joined with many.
And if it were something associated with them that could be grasped,
yet it is not grasped— if it were grasped, they would say, "We have perceived you there today," or "We [perceive you]. But it is not so.
And this is not the case; therefore, one does not go to another place in a dream. //2//
Furthermore, the objects seen in dreams are unreal because the non-existence of chariots and such is heard in accordance with reason.
By that very [means], the unreality of the dream has indeed been demonstrated; so they say.

The non-existence of chariots and other such things seen in dreams is heard in the Śruti, established through reasoning and logic, in the passage: "There are no chariots there" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10). The knowers of Brahman say that the apparent reality [of these objects], which was suggested by reasons such as their being located within the body and enclosed [by it], is clarified by that very Śruti which, while restating that [non-existence], is intent upon establishing the self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) in the dream state.
But because of their intermediate state, the distinctions [of objects] are known to exist there in the waking state;
as it is there, so it is in the dream state, though they differ by virtue of being concealed.
The proposition is that the objects perceived while awake are unreal. The reason is "because they are perceived. The example is "like the objects perceived in a dream.
Just as there is unreality for the objects perceived in that dream, so too in the waking state, the quality of being perceived is no different; this is the application of the reason.
Therefore, the conclusion is that even in the waking state, unreality is recognized. Because they exist within [the body] and are enclosed, dream-objects differ from waking-objects;
however, being objects of perception and being unreal are indistinguishable in both cases. //4//
For the wise say that the states of dreaming and waking are one, by reason of the very fact that the objects perceived in both are equally established as being unreal.

By means of the very well-known distinction between the grasped and the grasper as the cause, the wise declare the identity of the states of dream and waking on the basis of their equality; thus, this is the fruit of that which was already established by the preceding means of knowledge.
Furthermore, the unreality of the objects perceived in the waking state follows from their non-existence at the beginning and at the end.
That which does not exist in the beginning and at the end likewise does not exist in the present;
though they are similar to what is unreal, they are perceived as if they were real.
Whatever object does not exist at the beginning or at the end—such as a mirage and the like—is certainly non-existent even in its middle; so too are these various things perceived while awake.

Because they are absent at the beginning and the end, and because they are similar to false things such as mirages, they are indeed unreal. Nevertheless, they are perceived as if real by the deluded who do not know the self. (6)
START MandUpK 2.7:
As for the statement that the objects perceived in the waking state possess reality just like those perceived in a dream, that is untenable.

For it is observed that the objects of the waking state—such as food, drink, and vehicles—serve a purpose by effecting the cessation of hunger and thirst and performing functions such as going and coming.
But that [nature] does not belong to things seen in a dream;
therefore, the unreality of waking perceptions, like those seen in a dream, is a mere mental fabrication.
That is not so.
Why?
Because their purposiveness is contradicted in a dream;
therefore, they are indeed remembered as being false, like things at the beginning and the end.
The utility observed in food, drink, and so forth is contradicted in a dream.

For one who has eaten and drunk while awake and is satisfied, as soon as they fall asleep with their thirst quenched, they perceive themselves—having fasted for a day and night—as being afflicted by hunger and thirst even though they have eaten;
just as one who has eaten and drunk in a dream awakens feeling satisfied.

Therefore, since a contradiction is observed regarding things seen while awake when one is dreaming, we consider that their unreality—like that of dream-objects—is beyond doubt. Thus, the quality of having a beginning and an end is the same in both cases; indeed, they are remembered as being like falsehoods. //7//
START MandUpK 2.8:
As for the statement that the distinctions within the waking state are unreal because they are equal to the distinction between dreaming and waking, that is incorrect.
Why?
Because the example is unestablished.
How so? For these very distinctions perceived while awake are not seen in a dream.
What then?
One sees something unprecedented in a dream;
one considers oneself mounted upon an eight-tusked elephant with eight arms.

Whatever else of this kind one sees that is unprecedented in a dream, that is not equal to anything else that is non-existent; rather, it is indeed existent. Therefore, the illustrative example is unestablished.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the waking state is unreal like a dream.
That is not so; for that unprecedented thing which you consider to be seen in a dream is not established by itself.
What then?
For this is an unprecedented state, like that of the inhabitants of heaven;
having gone there, he perceives them just as one who is well-trained perceives things here on earth.
For this unprecedented state is indeed a property of the locus; it is a property of the seer who possesses the dream-state as his locus.
Just as Indra and others who dwell in heaven possess the quality of having a thousand eyes and so forth, so too is this unprecedented property of the dream-seer.
It is not established by itself like the essential nature of the seer.
This dreamer, having gone to the state of dreaming, perceives such unprecedented mental constructions of his own mind as these.
Just as in this world a well-trained traveler, having traveled to another region by that path, sees those objects there, so it is here.

Therefore, just as the dharmas of the dreamer—such as the rope-snake, the mirage, and so forth—are non-existent, so too the unprecedented things seen in the dream are merely the dharmas of the dreamer and are thus non-existent. Consequently, the analogy of the dream is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Having refuted the doubt regarding [the world] being unprecedented, he speaks again, elaborating on how the distinctions of the waking state are equal to a dream, stating:
"Even within the occurrence of a dream, that which is imagined internally by the mind is unreal."
If that which is grasped by the mind exists externally, then the unreality of these two is observed.

Even within the occurrence of a dream—that is, even in the state of dreaming—there is that which is unreal, mentally constructed through the internal mind’s desires; for immediately after the act of conceptualization, that very thing vanishes. Conversely, there is that which is real, such as a jar or similar object, perceived externally by the mind through the gates of the eyes and other senses.
Thus, even when one has determined with certainty that "this alone is true," a distinction between the real and the unreal is observed.
The unreality of both—whether conceived as internal or external—is indeed observed. //9//
Even during the waking state, that which is imagined internally by the mind is unreal, while that which is grasped externally by the mind is real; therefore, the unreality of these two is logical.

The unreality of both the existent and the non-existent is logical, because there is no distinction in their being mentally constructed internally and externally; the rest has been explained elsewhere. //10//
START MandUpK 2.11 The opponent says: If there is the unreality of both— the distinctions and the two states— then...
Who perceives these distinctions, and who indeed is their conceptualizer?
If the distinctions between the states of dreaming and waking are unreal, who perceives these things imagined within and without?
Who indeed is their conceptualizer?
The intended meaning is: what is the objective support for memory and cognition?
If the doctrine of selflessness is not accepted. //11//
The divine Self, by its own power of illusion (*māyā*), fashions itself as the self through itself;
it is that very same [Self] which perceives the various distinctions—this is the definitive conclusion of the Vedānta. (MandUpK 2.12)

By its own māyā, this Lord, through its own self, imagines within itself the forms of differentiation to be described hereafter—just as [one perceives] snakes and the like upon a rope—and likewise perceives those very differentiations by itself; such is the conclusion of the Vedānta.
The intention is that there is no other substratum for knowledge and memory, nor are knowledge and memory without a basis as the Nihilists (Vaināśikas) maintain. //12//
Regarding how one who forms a resolve (saṅkalpayan) constructs [it], it is said:
"He transforms other states of being (bhāva) that are established within the internal mind."
And the Lord likewise imagines those who are fixed [in their destiny] as being outside the mind itself.

The Lord—the Self, which is the meaning of "Īśvara"—fashions and produces various other worldly entities and objects, such as sound and so forth; others that are established within the mind in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and fixed, such as the earth and so on; and others that are unfixed, existing only at the time of conceptualization. Thus, while being outside the mind, he likewise fashions those characterized by mental desires and the like within the mind. This is how the Lord fashions them. //13//
START MandUpK 2.14:
It may be suspected that everything is mentally constructed like a dream;
for external objects, which are mutually distinguishable, possess a distinct characteristic from mental constructs such as desires, which are characterized by being determined solely by the mind.
That suspicion is not justified:

"For those things that have the duration of a moment of mind within, and those that have the duration of two moments without—all of them are merely imagined; their distinction is not caused by anything else. (MandUkK 2.14)

For those things which are "of the time of mind" (*cittakāla*) are internal and delimited by the mind; they are "of the time of mind" because there is no other delimiting time apart from the time of the mind.
The meaning is that they are perceived only at the very moment of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Furthermore, two time-periods and their distinct divisions are mutually delimiting:
for example, "he sits while milking the cow," meaning he milks the cow for as long as he sits, and he sits for as long as he milks the cow.

That "this is so much" and "that is so much"— such mutual relationship of delimiting and being delimited among external differentiated entities, whether they be internal mental moments or external temporal moments, all of these are merely imagined.
There is no external distinction of being two-fold in time that has any cause other than being imagined.
For here too, the analogy of a dream certainly applies. //14//
Those things which are indeed unmanifest within, and those which are indeed manifest without—
all these are merely imagined; the distinction, however, lies in the difference of the sense organs.

Furthermore, whether objects are internally unmanifest or manifest as mere mental impressions, or whether they appear clearly externally through other senses such as the eyes, that distinction is not caused by the actual existence of those diverse entities; for even in dreams, things are seen in that same way.
What, then, is the cause? It is solely produced by the different senses.
Therefore, it is established that even the states of waking and so forth are merely imagined, just like the states of a dream. //15//
START MandUpK 2.16:
Regarding the conceptualization of external and internal entities as being related to one another by way of cause and effect, it is asked: what is their root?
It is said: First, speech conceives of a living soul (jīva), and subsequently, various kinds of entities.
Just as there is ignorance regarding external and internal things, so too is there lack of mindfulness.

The individual soul (*jīva*), characterized by the notion "I am the cause and the effect" and "pleasure and pain are mine," previously imagined itself as such within the pure Self— which is not characterized in that way— just as one imagines a snake in a rope.

Thereupon, for the sake of that [Self], it imagines various states—such as actions, agents, and fruits—as well as external and internal entities like the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, through their differentiation.
Regarding this imagination, the question is asked: "What is the cause?
It is said: that very soul (jīva), which is self-imagined and authorized for all imagination, exists according to its ignorance (yathāvidya).
"One who has such knowledge and such discernment is 'yathāvidyaḥ';
one whose memory is of that same kind is 'tathāsmṛtiḥ'—thus he becomes.

Therefore, from the causal conceptualization-consciousness (hetu-kalpanā-vijñāna) arises the resultant consciousness; from that, the memory of cause and effect; from that, the consciousness of those [objects]; and from that, the various consciousnesses of their purposeful activity, their agents, and their distinct results."

From those [objects] arises memory of them; from that memory, again, arise cognitions of them. In this way, one conceptualizes external and internal things in manifold ways through the relationship of mutual cause and effect. //16//
START MandUpK 2.17:

It has been stated that the conceptualization of a living soul (*jīva*) is the root of all conceptualizations; [the author] now demonstrates by means of an illustration what the cause of that very conceptualization of a living soul is:
"Just as a rope, when not clearly ascertained in the darkness, is conceptually constructed..."
In the same way, the Self is conceptualized through states such as the appearance of a snake or a stream of water.

Just as in the world, when a rope in deep darkness has not been determined or ascertained as being "exactly this," it becomes the object of manifold conceptual constructions—such as "Is it a snake? "A stream of water? or "A staff?"—due to the prior lack of certainty regarding its own nature; for if the rope had already been ascertained in its own nature beforehand, [such misconceptions would not arise].
The conceptual construction of a snake and so forth would not have occurred with respect to one's own hand, fingers, and so on;
this is the illustration.

Likewise, because the self is not ascertained in its own nature—which is the non-dual reality of the existence of pure representation (*viśuddha-vijñaptimātra-sattā*)—as being distinct from the worthless phenomena of saṃsāra such as cause and effect, it is imagined by the self through the infinite varieties of states such as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Thus, this is the established conclusion of all the Upaniṣads. //17//
Just as when a rope has been definitively determined, conceptual construction ceases and there remains only the non-duality of "it is a rope," so too is the definitive realization of the Self.

Just as when there is the certainty "this is indeed a rope," all conceptual constructions cease and there remains the non-duality of "this is indeed a rope," so too, through the sun-like light of realized knowledge produced by the scripture that teaches the absence of all worldly attributes— expressed as "not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22)— one attains the certain realization of the Self: "All this is indeed the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2),
"without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).
"For it is without interior or exterior, indeed unborn" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2);
"Ageless, immortal, deathless, fearless" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25);
"One alone, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1). //18//
START MandUpK 2.19:

If it is certain that the Self is indeed one alone, how is it said to be differentiated by these infinite states characterized as transmigratory existence, such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth? Listen:
It is differentiated by these infinite states, such as the vital breaths and so forth.
This is the illusion of that God, by which he himself is deluded.

This is the illusion of that divine Self; just as an illusionist creates an illusion that makes the utterly pure sky appear as if filled with trees bearing blossoms and foliage, so too is this the illusion of the Divine, by which even he himself becomes,
as it were, deluded.
It has been stated: "My māyā is difficult to transcend" (Gītā 7.14). //19//

Those who know the vital breath (prāṇa) say it is the vital breath; those who know that [the elements] say it is the beings; those who know the qualities (guṇa) say it is the qualities; and those who know that [the principles] say it is the principles (tattva). (MandU 2.20)
Those who know the quarters say they are the quarters; those who know the objects say they are the objects;
those who know the worlds say they are the worlds; and those who know the gods say they are the gods. (MandU 2.21)

Those who know the Vedas say, "The Vedas"; those who know sacrifice say, "Sacrifice"; those who know the enjoyer say, "The enjoyer"; and those who know the object of enjoyment say, "The object of enjoyment. (MandU 2.22)
"It is subtle," say those who know it as subtle; "it is gross," say those who know it as gross;
"it is embodied," say those who know it as embodied; and "it is formless," say those who know it as formless. (MandU 2.23)
Those who know time call it "time"; those who know the quarters call them "the quarters";
those who know arguments call them "arguments"; and those who know the worlds call them "the worlds. (MandUkK 2.24)

Those who know it as the mind call it *manas*; those who know it as the intellect call it *buddhi*; those who know it as the heart call it *citta*; and those who know it call it merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). (MandU 2.25)
Some say it consists of twenty-five principles, others of twenty-six;
some say it consists of thirty-one, and others that it is infinite. (MandUk 2.26)

Those who know the world call the worlds "stages of life" (āśramas); those who know that [reality] call them "gender" (liṅga)—as female, male, and neuter—while others call them "the higher and the lower. (MandUk 2.27)
Those who know creation call it "creation"; those who know dissolution call it "dissolution";
and those who know persistence call it "persistence"—yet all these are always [one] here.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the wise one whose essence is the seed; the others, from the individual self (*sthātṛ*) onwards, are indeed its various effects.

Furthermore, all other worldly distinctions imagined by all living beings—such as the snake and so forth imagined upon a rope—are imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) because of the failure to ascertain the true nature of the Self within the Self that is devoid of them. This is the summarized meaning of the verses beginning with "the vital breath.
No effort has been made to provide a word-by-word commentary on each term, because such an endeavor would be of little utility and because the meanings of the terms are already established. //28//
What more need be said?
Whatever state of being one shows to another, that very state of being the other perceives.
And having become that very thing, he protects it; that grasping then approaches him.

If the teacher or another authoritative person (āpta) should point out any other state or entity—whether one of those already mentioned, such as the vital breaths (prāṇa), or one not yet mentioned—saying, "This alone is reality," then the disciple perceives that state as his own self, thinking "I am this" or "this is mine.
And that pointed-out state protects the seer; having become that very state, it guards him.
One obstructs [the mind] from all sides by means of one's own self;
"grasping at that" (tad-graha) is attachment to that,
which is precisely this very [clinging].
The word "tattvam" (the reality) approaches that grasper;
the meaning is that it enters into his very being. //29//
By these non-distinct entities, this [Self] is characterized as if it were distinct. He who knows this according to reality may form such a conception without hesitation. (MandU 2.30)

The meaning is this: by these [faculties] beginning with *prāṇa*, which are non-different from the Self and whose nature is non-separation, this Self is perceived, characterized, and determined as if it were distinct—just as a rope is perceived as having the forms of imagined entities such as a snake—by the deluded.

However, for those who possess discrimination, the intention is that just as snakes and the like are imagined upon a rope, the *prāṇas* and so forth do not exist apart from the Self; for there is the Śruti: "All this is what this Self is" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.4.6, 4.5.7).

Thus, the non-existence of things apart from the Self—of those imagined within the Self like a snake on a rope—and the fact that the Self alone is absolute and free from conceptual differentiation, [are established].

He who knows [the Veda] according to its true nature through both scripture and reasoning may, free from doubt, determine the meaning of the Veda according to its divisions— meaning he determines it, thinking, "This sentence has this as its purport," or "That has another as its purport. For one who does not know the inner self (adhyātma) is not able to know the Vedas in their true essence.
"For no one who is ignorant of the inner self enjoys the fruit of ritual action"—such indeed is the statement of Manu (Manusmṛti 6.82). //30//

START MandUpK 2.31: That which was stated through reasoning regarding the non-existence of duality is now declared to be understood through the authority of the Vedānta: "Just as a dream, an illusion, or a city of the Gandharvas is perceived..."
In this same way, this entire universe is perceived by the wise in the Vedāntas.
Dream and illusion—dream and illusion consist of unreal things and are false, yet they appear as if they consisted of real things to those who lack discernment.

Just as a city of the Gandharvas, which appears crowded with spread-out merchandise, marketplaces, palaces, women, and people, is seen to suddenly vanish into non-existence while being perceived as real;
and just as dreams and illusions are seen to be of an unreal nature.
Likewise, this entire dualistic universe is seen as unreal;
where? He says: in the Vedāntas—"There is not the slightest diversity here" (KaU 2.1.11).
(11, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19) “Indra by means of his powers of illusion” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19);
“In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.1).
17) “In the beginning, Brahman alone was this” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10);
“Verily, from a second there arises fear” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.2); “But there is no second for it” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).

23) Regarding such passages as, “Where everything has become one’s very self” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15), the meaning is that by the wise— those who are discerning and capable of perceiving the reality of things with extreme subtlety—
it is seen as resembling a dark abyss, like a bubble on the rain.
"Consisting mostly of destruction, devoid of happiness, and followed by destruction, it leads to non-existence"—thus says the Smṛti of Vyāsa. //31//
START MandUpK 2.32 This verse serves to summarize the meaning of the section:
when duality is unreal and the Self alone exists as the ultimate reality, then it follows that all this worldly and Vedic activity has its sphere solely within ignorance (*avidyā*). At that time—
There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one bound nor one who practices,
neither one seeking liberation nor one liberated— this is the ultimate truth.
Cessation is not the act of ceasing; cessation is dissolution. Origination is birth. The bound one is the transmigrating individual soul (jīva).
The practitioner possesses the means for liberation;
the seeker of liberation desires release;
the liberated one is freed from bondage.
Because there is an absence of both arising and dissolution, those such as the bound do not exist; this is the ultimate reality.
How is there an absence of arising and dissolution? It is said:
Because duality is non-existent; for it is said:
"Where there is, as it were, duality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14), and "He who sees here, as it were, multiplicity" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.1.11).
10,11) “All this is indeed the Self” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2); “All this is indeed Brahman” (Nṛsiṃhottaratāpanīya Upaniṣad 7);
“One only, without a second” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2).
1) From various scriptural passages such as "All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6; 4.5.7), the unreality of duality is established.
For origination or dissolution can belong only to that which exists, not to that which does not exist, such as the horns of a hare.
Nor does non-duality arise or dissolve;
for it is a contradiction to say that the non-dual possesses arising and dissolution.
Furthermore, it has been stated that the conventional practice of duality is merely imagined within the Self—characterized by vital breath and so forth—just like the snake [imagined] in a rope.
For there is neither dissolution nor origination of the mental construction characterized as a "rope-snake" and so forth, either in the rope, nor in the mind,
nor in both;
likewise, because non-duality is not distinct from being mental.
For indeed, when the mind is restrained or in deep sleep, duality is not perceived;
therefore, it is established that duality is merely a mental construction.
Consequently, it is well said that because duality is non-existent, its cessation and so forth do not exist in the ultimate sense.

If this is so, then the operation of the scripture would apply to the absence of duality and not to non-duality itself, because that would involve a contradiction. And such being the case, since there would be no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the reality of non-duality, it would follow that non-duality is a void,
as duality itself is absent.

"No; this has already been refuted by the argument that it is impossible for a conceptual construction (vikalpanā) such as a snake in a rope to be without a basis. How then do you revive this [objection]? To this he says: "The rope itself, being the basis for the conceptual construction of the snake, is itself merely conceptualized.
Thus, the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is untenable. "No; because when conceptualization ceases, that which is non-conceptualized exists precisely by virtue of its being non-conceptualized."

If it is argued that [the world] is non-existent like a snake on a rope, we say no; because it is absolutely unconstructed (*avikalpita*), just like the portion of the rope prior to the cognition of the absence of the snake.
Furthermore, since the existence of the constructor (*vikalpayitṛ*) is admitted to be established prior to the arising of the construction, its non-existence is untenable.
But how, then, can the scripture bring about the cessation of the cognition of duality if it lacks any operation upon its own nature?
This is not a fault;
for duality is superimposed upon the Self through ignorance, just as a snake is [superimposed] upon a rope.

How so? [Such notions as] "I am happy," "I am miserable," "I am deluded," "I am born," "I have died," "I am aged," "I possess a body," "I see," "I am manifest," "I am unmanifest," "I am the agent," "I am the enjoyer of fruits," "I am joined," "I am disjoined," "I am decayed," "I am grown old," and "this belongs to me"—all these are superimposed upon the Self. This is because the Self is present in all of them, never deviating from them.
Just as a rope [is the reality] amidst various distinctions such as a snake or a stream;
and since the cognition of the true nature of the qualified object is thus already established, it is not something to be produced by the scripture.
Furthermore, a scripture that attempts to produce what has not been produced is invalid if it merely imitates what has already been accomplished.

Since the Self does not abide in its own true nature solely due to the obstruction caused by specific qualities such as happiness superimposed by ignorance, and since abiding in one's own true nature is the highest good (*śreyas*), the scripture— by means of statements such as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) and "neither gross nor subtle" (*asthūla* etc.)— produces the cognition of the absence of happiness and so forth in the Self, thereby removing [the notion of] happiness and the like.
Just like the nature of the self (*ātman*), the quality of being unhappy and so forth does not persist across the various distinctions such as happiness and so forth.
If it were to persist, then there would be no specific distinction characterized by superimposed happiness and so forth,
just as coldness cannot exist in fire which possesses the specific quality of heat.
Therefore, it is established that qualities such as happiness are merely imagined within the Self, which is in fact devoid of all distinctions.
As for the scriptural teaching regarding the Self's lack of happiness and so forth, its purpose is solely to negate those specific qualities like happiness; thus it is proven.
This is the aphorism of the knowers of the tradition: "But [the scripture] is established [as authoritative] because it serves to negate [false attributes]. (32)
START MandUpK 2.33 He states the reason for the meaning of the preceding verse:
"This [world] is imagined through non-existent entities and through non-duality."
Therefore, even entities are indeed non-dual; thus, non-duality is auspicious.

Just as upon a rope, by means of unreal things such as a snake, a stream, or a staff, and by means of the real substance that is the rope—which is non-dual—the very substance of the rope is imagined as "this is a snake," "this is a stream," or "this is a staff"—so too, by means of the infinite, unreal, and non-existent [entities] such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), [the Self is imagined];
for it does not exist in ultimate reality. Indeed, when the mind is not moving, no state whatsoever can be perceived by anyone;
and there is no movement of the Self.
Since the entities perceived as being in motion cannot be conceived as existing in an ultimate sense,

it follows that this very Self has been imagined by itself— through the non-existent entities such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and through the non-dual ultimately real Self— as the locus of all conceptual constructions, just like a rope [is imagined to be a snake].
Although it possesses a single, eternal nature,
those states such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth are likewise conceptualized by means of that very non-dual, eternal self;
for no conceptualization is ever found to exist without a basis.
Therefore, because it is the locus of all conceptual constructions and because non-duality is never otherwise, non-duality remains auspicious even during the state of conceptualization;
conceptualizations themselves, however, are inauspicious,
for they cause fear and the like, just as [the perception of] a snake in a rope does.
Because it is non-dual and free from fear, that very [nature] is auspicious. //33//
Furthermore, from what source does auspicious non-duality arise?
From that which has become manifold.
Wherever the separateness of one thing from another is perceived, there misfortune arises.
Those who know reality understand that this manifold world does not exist by way of its own nature, nor by itself in any way; nothing is either separate or non-separate. (MandUkK 2.34)

For here, in this non-dual Self which is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*), this entire world—the collection of transmigratory existence beginning with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—when examined as its own nature, that is, as its ultimate form, does not become a plurality of distinct entities.
Just as a superimposed snake, when defined by the manifestation of the rope's true nature, does not exist as something diverse, so it is here.
Nor does this [world] exist by way of its own nature as the vital breaths and so forth.

Because they are merely imagined, like a snake in a rope, at no time do the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth exist as separate entities from one another, just as a buffalo exists separately from a horse.
Therefore, let it be that nothing exists as separate from food, nor from each other, nor from the Supreme; thus do the Brahmins who know the truth of the ultimate reality understand.
Therefore, because it lacks the cause of inauspiciousness, the intended meaning is that non-duality itself is auspicious (śiva). //34//
This very right vision is praised by sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and are free from passion, fear, and anger: MandUpK 2.35.
For this is seen to be free from conceptual construction, the stilling of all manifold proliferation, and non-dual.

The Self, which is free from all defects such as passion, fear, hatred, and anger, has been seen—that is, realized—by sages who are always contemplative, discerning, masters of the Vedas, knowers of the true essence of the Vedic meaning, and possessed of wisdom; it is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), devoid of all mental constructs (*śūnya*), and the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañcopaśama*).
The "phenomenal world" (*prapañca*) is the expansion of duality and differentiation; its "cessation" (*upaśama*) is its non-existence within that Self. Therefore, the Self is non-dual (*advaya*).

The intended meaning is that the Supreme Self can be perceived only by those who are free from defects—learned renunciants devoted to the true meaning of the Vedānta—and not by others, such as logicians and the like, whose minds are defiled by passion and other afflictions and whose views are biased toward their own particular positions. //35//

START MandUpK 2.36 Since it is non-dual, auspicious, and fearless because its nature is the pacification of all misfortunes, therefore, having known it thus, one should apply one's mindfulness to non-duality.
Having fully realized non-duality, one should conduct oneself in the world like an insentient object.
Therefore, having understood this in such a way, one should apply mindfulness to non-duality (*advaita*).
The meaning is that one should cultivate mindfulness solely for the sake of realizing non-duality.

Having realized that non-duality and known "I am the Supreme Brahman," one should—having directly and immediately realized the unborn Self which transcends hunger and other needs and is beyond all worldly transaction—conduct oneself in the world like an insentient object.
The intention is that he does not proclaim himself, thinking, "I am such a person. //36//
Regarding the question, "By what conduct should one move through the world? it is said:
"Free from praise, free from salutation, and indeed free from the utterance of *svadhā*."
And the ascetic, whose dwelling is unstable, should be one who accepts whatever comes by chance.

The intended meaning is that he has abandoned all external desires and has undertaken the wandering life of a paramahaṃsa, being free from all ritual actions such as praise and salutation; for there is the scriptural testimony beginning with, "Having known this very Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.13),
and [the words of the Gītā], "With their intellects fixed on That, with That as their Self, established in That, having That as their supreme goal" (Gītā 5.17).
17) And from such Smṛti passages as these, [it follows that] the body is mobile because it undergoes change at every moment, whereas the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is immobile.
At any time, for the sake of activities such as eating, the reality of the Self remains an immobile essence like space; it is the abode, the support, and the locus of the Self.
When, through forgetfulness, he thinks "I am," then his body is his moving abode; thus, this wise man has a moving-and-unmoving abode, and is no longer dependent on external objects.
Furthermore, he should be "content with whatever comes" (yādṛcchika), meaning his maintenance of the body consists merely of a loincloth for covering and food obtained by chance. //37//
Having perceived the reality of the internal self and having perceived the reality of the external world,
one becomes that very reality; delighting therein, one shall not fall away from that reality.

The external reality consisting of earth and the other elements, as well as the internal reality characterized by the body and so forth, are unreal—like a snake in a rope, or like a dream and an illusion—according to such scriptural passages as: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4).

The Self, however, including both the external and the internal, is indeed unborn, without predecessor, without interior, without exterior, whole, all-pervading like space, subtle, immovable, devoid of qualities, partless, and actionless; "That is the Truth, That is the Self, That art thou" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).

Thus, according to the scripture [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 8/16], having seen reality in this way, one becomes that reality; delighting in that, one does not delight in the external. Just as someone who perceives reality as it is, having accepted the mind as the self, considers the self to have moved along with the movement of the mind, so too [one who has not realized] considers the self—which is actually the body and so forth—to have moved from its true nature.
Sometimes he thinks, "I have now fallen away from the reality of the Self";
and when the mind is concentrated, he sometimes thinks that his self has become serene and that "now I have become the reality.
At such times, he would not be a knower of the Self.

Because the Self is of a single nature and because its deviation from its own nature is impossible, the intention is that one should always remain undeviated from the realization "I am Brahman," and thus become one who perceives the reality of the Self as eternally undeviated. As it is said: "The wise see with an equal eye toward both a dog and an outcaste" (Gītā 5.18), and "The same in all beings" (Gītā 13.27).
17) Because of such traditional authority (smṛti), [as stated in verse] 38.
